paragraphs: In Merthyr Tydfil the council's own fostering service is Foster Wales Merthyr Tydfil, a not-for-profit service within the county borough council's children's services and one of the 22 Welsh council fostering services that make up Foster Wales. Its small team works from the Civic Centre on Castle Street and aims to keep local children in the communities, schools and friendships they already know. Children from Merthyr are also looked after by the services shown above.

The council service recruits for short-term care, which can last from one night to a year or more, and for long-term care that gives a child a settled home. It also looks for short-break carers, parent and child carers, therapeutic carers who get an extra layer of guidance, and carers for young refugees, more than 100 of whom arrive in Wales each year.

Foster Wales Merthyr Tydfil says its carers currently receive between £12,584 and £39,520 a year, depending on the type of fostering, how many children they look after and for how long. Approved carers on an additional allowance can get a 50% incentive payment towards their council tax, and the whole household gets free use of council gyms, pools and classes. Training comes through e-learning, podcasts and workshops with a full-time training officer, and newer carers can be mentored by experienced ones. Support groups, including one for men who foster, coffee mornings and school holiday activities sit alongside 24-hour support.

Across Wales the minimum weekly allowance for 2026-27 runs from £208 to £260 depending on the child's age, with any fee for the carer paid on top. Our Wales page sets out the national picture, and our Rhondda Cynon Taf and Caerphilly pages cover the neighbouring areas. Speak to Foster Wales Merthyr Tydfil and to one or two of the services above, and ask each what it pays and how it supports carers.
